notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a hand can be partitioned into groups of groupSize consecutive integers.
Idea: Count card frequencies and repeatedly start a group at the smallest remaining value.
Technique and why it applies: Each group must begin with the smallest remaining card; the algorithm consumes one copy of each successive number and removes exhausted minima from the heap.
Invariant: freq records unused copies and min_heap contains values that were present initially.
Edge cases: collections and heapq are used without imports in the snippet. If groupSize is zero, modulo raises an error; the input constraint requires a positive size.
Complexity: Heap operations and frequency updates take O(n log n) time and O(n) space, broadly matching the author's labels.

Task and constraints: Check whether all cards can be rearranged into consecutive groups of size W.
Idea: Count card values, heapify all cards, and consume W consecutive values for each group.
Technique and why it applies: Each iteration chooses the smallest still-needed card and decrements counts for the sequence starting there. Negative counts indicate a missing duplicate or invalid group.
Invariant: counts stores remaining multiplicities; the heap provides a small candidate start while zero-count entries are skipped.
Edge cases: The heap contains duplicates, but only the initial number of groups is processed. If counts are inconsistent, negative counts cause False.
Complexity: Heap construction and removals are O(n log n), with O(n) frequency and heap storage.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest walk that visits every node in an undirected graph.
Idea: Compute all-pairs shortest distances, then memoize the best cost to visit a bitmask of remaining nodes.
Technique and why it applies: Floyd-Warshall supplies distances between any two nodes. The recursive state chooses the next required node and adds its shortest-path distance to the remaining tour.
Invariant: fn(x,mask) is intended to be the minimum cost from x to visit every node set in mask.
Edge cases: inf and cache are used without imports. More importantly, mask is cleared by visiting a node, but the recursion does not track nodes traversed along shortest paths separately; the method's decomposition should be validated against revisits.
Complexity: Floyd-Warshall is O(n³), and memoized subset states take O(n²2^n) time and O(n2^n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of edges in a walk visiting all graph nodes, allowing repeated visits.
Idea: Run multi-source BFS over states consisting of a visited-node bitmask and current node.
Technique and why it applies: Every node is a possible start with a one-bit mask. Each edge adds a neighbor to the mask, and BFS reaches states in increasing path length.
Invariant: dp[mask][node] is the shortest known length for reaching node after visiting the nodes in mask.
Edge cases: The graph is assumed nonempty and connected, as in the problem. The first visit to each state is shortest because all edges have unit weight.
Complexity: There are O(n2^n) states and O(n2^n) transitions for bounded degree, using O(n2^n) time and space.

Task and constraints: Apply cumulative rightward shifts to each character of a lowercase string.
Idea: Compute suffix sums of shifts modulo 26, then shift each character by its corresponding total.
Technique and why it applies: Position i is affected by every shift from i onward, so the reverse cumulative sum gives the net alphabet rotation.
Invariant: nums[i] is the sum of shifts[i:] modulo 26.
Edge cases: The code repeatedly subtracts 26 until the character code is in range; shifts are assumed nonnegative, and lowercase input is assumed.
Complexity: Two linear passes take O(n) time and O(n) extra space.

Task and constraints: Shift each character by the sum of all shift amounts from its index to the end.
Idea: Maintain a running suffix total modulo 26 while scanning left to right.
Technique and why it applies: The initial total is sum(shifts), and after processing each character the current shift amount is removed, leaving the suffix sum for the next index.
Invariant: times is the net shift applying to the current character, modulo 26.
Edge cases: Empty strings produce empty output. The code assumes S and shifts have equal length.
Complexity: Computing the sum and scanning characters take O(n) time and O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Choose an empty seat maximizing the distance to the nearest occupied seat.
Idea: Find occupied positions and compare leading/trailing empty runs with the midpoint distance of each interior gap.
Technique and why it applies: At an interior gap, sitting near its center maximizes the minimum distance to either occupied endpoint; at the ends, the entire empty run is available.
Invariant: seat_nums stores occupied indices in increasing order.
Edge cases: If no seat is occupied, min and max on seat_nums fail. The usual problem guarantees at least one occupied seat.
Complexity: Scanning and calculating gaps take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Maximize distance from a chosen empty seat to the nearest occupied seat.
Idea: Track the previous occupied index and update the best distance for each gap.
Technique and why it applies: The leading gap's best distance is its length; an interior gap contributes half its width rounded down, and the trailing gap contributes its full length.
Invariant: prev is the most recent occupied seat, and result is the best distance found so far.
Edge cases: If every seat is empty, the method returns len(seats), but the problem normally guarantees an occupied seat. The initial result of one is superseded by the end-gap check when appropriate.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the union area of axis-aligned rectangles modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Sweep horizontal events while a segment tree maintains the total covered x-length.
Technique and why it applies: Each rectangle adds coverage at its lower y and removes it at its upper y. Between event heights, area increases by vertical distance times current covered width.
Invariant: st.total[1] is the covered horizontal length at the current sweep height.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used without import. The tree uses compressed elementary intervals, but the call's upper boundary is len(xs)-1 while the represented interval indices end at len(xs)-2, so the recursion bounds deserve scrutiny.
Complexity: Coordinate compression and event sorting take O(n log n), with O(n log n) segment-tree updates and O(n) storage.

Task and constraints: Calculate the total union area of rectangles using a horizontal sweep line.
Idea: Sort rectangle opening/closing events and maintain active x-coverage in a dynamic segment tree.
Technique and why it applies: Covered width times the vertical distance since the previous event adds the strip area. Range updates adjust coverage counts, and a positive count marks a fully covered segment.
Invariant: The root total is the union length of active x-intervals between the current and next event heights.
Edge cases: Empty rectangles make events[0] fail. The dynamic tree creates child nodes lazily, and interval endpoints are compressed to half-open index ranges.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n); segment-tree updates are O(log n) per event, giving O(n log n) time and O(n log n) tree storage.

Task and constraints: For each person, find the quietest person who is at least as rich as them.
Idea: Topologically process the richer-than directed graph, propagating the quietest known candidate from richer nodes to poorer neighbors.
Technique and why it applies: Edges point from richer to poorer. When processing a node, its best candidate is compared with each poorer neighbor's current candidate before that neighbor becomes ready.
Invariant: arr[v] is the quietest person known among v and all richer ancestors processed so far.
Edge cases: collections is used without import. The code assumes the richer relation is acyclic, as guaranteed by the problem.
Complexity: Topological traversal is O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space.

Task and constraints: Find the peak index in an array that strictly increases and then strictly decreases.
Idea: Binary-search for the boundary where values stop increasing.
Technique and why it applies: If arr[mid] is less than arr[mid+1], the peak lies to the right; otherwise it lies at mid or left.
Invariant: beg and end bracket the possible peak position.
Edge cases: When mid reaches the last index, arr[mid+1] can be out of range. The loop allows end to equal the last index, so the implementation can raise IndexError.
Complexity: Intended time is O(log n) and space O(1), but the boundary bug prevents reliable execution.

Task and constraints: Return the peak index of a mountain array with a strictly increasing prefix and decreasing suffix.
Idea: Binary-search based on whether the midpoint is on the ascending or descending slope.
Technique and why it applies: On the ascending slope, move left beyond mid; on the descending slope, move right below mid. The converged left pointer is the peak boundary.
Invariant: left advances while the peak is to its right, and right retreats while the peak is at or to its left.
Edge cases: arr[mid+1] can be out of bounds if mid is the final index; with valid mountain constraints, the search path usually keeps mid before the last index, but this should be checked.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count car fleets that arrive at a target without passing one another.
Idea: Sort cars from nearest to farthest from the target and compare their arrival times.
Technique and why it applies: A car behind a slower fleet joins it if its arrival time is no greater than the fleet's; a strictly later arrival forms a new fleet.
Invariant: arrival_bound is the arrival time of the slowest fleet ahead encountered so far.
Edge cases: The condition not arrival_bound treats a zero arrival time as unset, but cars are assumed to start before the target. Equal arrival times merge into the fleet ahead.
Complexity: Sorting dominates at O(n log n), with O(n) storage for zipped cars.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of swaps needed to transform s1 into s2, where they are anagrams.
Idea: Recursively fix the first mismatched position by swapping in a character that matches the target there.
Technique and why it applies: At index i, if current already matches s2, recursion advances; otherwise candidates with the needed target character are tried and the minimum swap count is cached.
Invariant: Positions before i are intended to match s2, and dp[i][curr] stores the best remaining swaps for that state.
Edge cases: sys.maxsize is used without importing sys. The memo state includes the full current string, but the recursion can still explore many equivalent swaps; it assumes s1 and s2 are anagrams.
Complexity: The search is exponential in the worst case, with memo space proportional to explored (index,string) states.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps to make A equal B when they are anagrams.
Idea: Use BFS over strings, swapping the first mismatched character with a later character that matches B at that position.
Technique and why it applies: Correcting the first mismatch avoids exploring swaps that disturb already-correct prefixes. BFS finds the minimum number of swaps because each swap is one edge.
Invariant: Each queued string is reachable in the current number of swaps, and lookup prevents duplicate states.
Edge cases: neighbors assumes a mismatch exists; if s already equals B, the outer loop returns before calling it. The code does not initially add A to lookup, allowing a possible duplicate state.
Complexity: State space can be factorial in string length, so worst-case time and space are exponential.

Task and constraints: Compute the score of a balanced parentheses string using the rule ()=1, concatenation adds, and enclosing parentheses doubles.
Idea: Track nesting depth and add the weight of each primitive pair.
Technique and why it applies: When a closing parenthesis immediately follows an opening one, the pair contributes 2^(level-1), which is the score of a primitive pair nested at that depth.
Invariant: level is the current nesting depth and result accumulates contributions from every immediate pair.
Edge cases: The code assumes a valid balanced string. Nested structures contribute through their innermost primitive pairs, and empty input returns zero.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Evaluate the score of a balanced parentheses string.
Idea: Use a stack of scores for nested parentheses, combining each closed group into its parent.
Technique and why it applies: Opening parentheses push a fresh score. On closing, an empty pair scores one, while a nonempty pair doubles its inner score; that value is added to the enclosing level.
Invariant: Each stack entry stores the accumulated score at one nesting level.
Edge cases: The input must be balanced and nonempty parentheses are not otherwise required. Invalid closing parentheses can pop the root and cause an error.
Complexity: Each character triggers one stack operation, giving O(n) time and O(n) worst-case space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the score of a balanced parentheses string under the recursive scoring rules.
Idea: Count nesting depth and add a power of two whenever an immediate () pair closes.
Technique and why it applies: A primitive pair nested at depth d contributes 2^d after depth is decremented; concatenated components add their contributions.
Invariant: depth tracks open parentheses before the current character, and result accumulates completed primitive contributions.
Edge cases: The code assumes valid balanced input. For the first character being a closing parenthesis, s[i-1] would wrap to the final character, so malformed strings are not handled.
Complexity: One scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Minimize total wages paid to hire exactly k workers under the rule that every worker is paid the same wage-to-quality ratio.
Idea: Sort workers by wage/quality ratio and maintain the k smallest qualities among candidates seen so far.
Technique and why it applies: For a chosen ratio, total pay is ratio times total quality. A max-heap encoded with negative qualities lets the algorithm replace the largest quality with a smaller one.
Invariant: pq contains the selected workers' qualities and kSmallest is their total quality.
Edge cases: heapq and heappop/heappush are not imported in the snippet. The loop begins at c=k, so it tests every later ratio after initializing the first k workers.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n) and heap updates O(n log k), with O(n+k) space.
